title: Unto us a child (Isaiah 9:2–7)
hook: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light

segments.voice: Yesterday, swords into ploughshares, and your line was study war no more. What peaceful act did you choose? Day four hundred sixty-five.

In December, in concert halls and churches in many countries, a choir waits for a particular chorus. The violins start running, light and quick. Then the voices come in, one part after another, tossing the same words back and forth. And then the whole choir lands, all together, on a string of names, hammered out one at a time. Handel wrote it in London, and it was first heard in Dublin in 1742. But the words weren't his. They come from the prophet Isaiah, written more than seven centuries before Jesus, to a kingdom with an army on its border. Today, the people who walked in darkness.
screen: `A CHOIR STANDS IN DECEMBER.` → `A STRING OF NAMES, HAMMERED OUT.` → `THE WORDS ARE ISAIAH'S.`

segments.voice: Isaiah's world was dark in a literal way. The Assyrian empire was on the march, and the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up around the Sea of Galilee, were among the first to be overrun. Into that, Isaiah says, in the King James Bible: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." Notice the tense. Have seen. The prophet speaks of the rescue as if it's already happened. Then he names the light: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace." Not a general. Not a weapon. A baby. The boots of the soldiers, Isaiah says, will be burned as fuel for the fire. And this child's peace will have no end, on the throne of David. Who is the child? Here readers differ, and it's worth saying plainly. Many Jewish readers have understood it as a royal child of Isaiah's own time, often King Hezekiah, or as a future king of David's line. Christians, from the Gospels on, read it as Jesus. Matthew's Gospel quotes this very passage when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first place the darkness fell. For Christians, the light rose exactly where the shadow had begun. That's why these words come back every Christmas: a child, given, into a dark place.
screen: `ASSYRIA, AND A DARK NORTH.` · `HAVE SEEN: SPOKEN AS IF DONE.` · `NOT A GENERAL. A CHILD.` · `GALILEE, WHERE THE SHADOW FELL.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS HAVE SEEN A GREAT LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle, or picture one. If you can, light a real one and set it in front of you. If not, imagine it clearly. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame. Notice how small it is, and how much of the room it changes. Then think of one dark place you know about right now: a family going through something, a city in the news, a corner of your own life. Hold the flame and that place together in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for that place by name. The bell holds the time.
Unto us a child. Isaiah's promise of a child born for a people in darkness, which Christians read as the birth of Jesus.
Your line: a great light. Today, be a small one: bring one bit of light into a place that feels dark for someone, a call, a kind word, a visit. Day four hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Isaiah 9:2–7 is one of the most common readings at Christmas services, including the traditional service of lessons and carols, and many Christians light candles through Advent while waiting for Christmas.

original.note: Hebrew: for a child has been born to us.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Christmas carol line.
what it means: a promise of a child-king, given to a people under the shadow of war.
what a scholar hears: the verbs are in the Hebrew perfect, speaking of the future as already done. Hebrew Bibles number these verses 9:1–6, one off from English.

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): the hook said a choir 'stands up' for this chorus (standing is the audience custom for the Hallelujah chorus, not For unto us a child is born) and gave an order of voice entries from memory; both simplified. Messiah dates (London 1741, Dublin 1742) unchanged; confirm.
Handel's Messiah: composed in London in 1741, first performed in Dublin, April 1742. The order of voice entries in the chorus (sopranos, tenors, altos, basses) is from memory; confirm or simplify.
Assyrian campaign against Zebulun and Naphtali (Tiglath-pileser III, c. 733–732 BC; 2 Kings 15:29). Confirm.
Jewish readings: Hezekiah (Talmud, Sanhedrin 94a) or a future Davidic king; presented without ranking. Confirm fair.
Prophetic perfect: Hebrew perfect verbs used for a future event spoken as complete. Confirm.
Verse numbering: Hebrew Bible 8:23–9:6 corresponds to English 9:1–7. Confirm the trapdoor's 'one off'.
Original-language line כִּי־יֶלֶד יֻלַּד־לָנוּ (9:5 Hebrew / 9:6 English). Confirm pointing and transliteration.
